summary:
I developed an interactive 2D/3D space mission simulation game using GDevelop for the NASA Space Apps Challenge's Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players step into the role of a NASA mission engineer tasked with designing and launching a spacecraft to Mars while managing real-world engineering constraints.
In the game, players select from modular spacecraft components, balancing fuel tank capacity and power generation systems like solar arrays versus nuclear batteries, with  a strict $500M mission budget and minimum power requirements. Once made, players launch their rocket to Mars. Alongside the core builder, the game I made includes a NASA Fun Facts section that teaches real aerospace principles, such as the tyranny of the rocket equation and deep-space power limits.
This project is important because it transforms complex aerospace systems engineering into an accessible, hands-on experience. By letting players test trade-offs between cost and capability in an engaging format, it inspires curiosity in STEM and helps learners understand the real decision-making challenges NASA engineers face when planning space exploration.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
My project is a Mars rocket building game where you play as a NASA engineer with a $500M budget. You start on a mission screen, then go to the rocket building bay where you pick parts to upgrade your rocket: Small Tanks ($100M), Heavy Tanks ($250M), Solar Panels ($100M), and Nuclear Batteries ($250M). Every time you buy a part, your budget goes down and your fuel or power goes up. When you finish spending your money, you press Launch to see if your rocket actually has enough fuel and power to survive the trip and land safely on Mars, or if the mission fails.

What benefits does it have?

Makes rocket science easy to understand: Instead of doing boring math, you get to see how fuel, power, and money actually affect a space mission.Fun to test and retry: If your rocket crashes or runs out of fuel, you can go straight back and try a different combo of parts.

What is the intended impact of the project?
I wanted to show other students and people my age that launching a rocket to Mars isn't just about building the biggest rocket—NASA engineers have to be really careful with their budget and pick the right parts so they don't run out of power or fuel halfway there.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? GDevelop: Used to build the whole game, make the buttons work, and keep track of the money, fuel, and power using global variables. Canva: Used to make my demo presentation slides. NASA Websites: Looked up real NASA info about rocket fuel tanks, solar panels, and nuclear batteries (RTGs) used on Mars rovers. AI Tools: Used GDevelop built-in AI and an AI chat helper to fix some of my event logic and help organize my project notes. Hardware: Just my laptop to build, test, and record the game.

How is your project creative?
Most space games are just flying around and dodging asteroids, so I wanted to make a game about actually planning the rocket before it even takes off. Making the upgrades cost $100M and $250M with only $500M total turns it into a cool strategy puzzle where you can't just buy everything.

What factors did your team consider? Real NASA tech vs. fun gameplay: I based the parts on real things NASA uses (like nuclear batteries vs. solar panels on Mars), while keeping the numbers simple so anyone can play right away. Game balance: I made sure you can't just click every button and win easily, you actually have to think about balancing fuel and power.
